newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania opposition demoralised under emergency.
newsitem.headline: Albania opposition demoralised under emergency.

text.p: Opponents of Albanian President Sali Berisha have joined forces in an 11-party alliance dominated by the former communists, but appear leaderless and demoralised by the imposition of emergency rule.

Berisha's Democratic Party won praise from international financial institutions after first taking power in 1992, but has since admitted it failed to warn investors off shady investment schemes, the initial trigger of the latest unrest.

The Democrats have also been accused by the opposition -- and many Western countries -- of vote-rigging and intimidation in winning re-election last year. Opposition parties boycotted the polls and refused to take up the handful of seats they won.
But the opposition, grouped in a Forum for Democracy, has failed to exploit popular discontent among investors who lost their life savings in the collapse of the pyramid schemes.
Although Berisha has accused the Socialists, the Forum's main component, of fomenting "armed rebellion", most opposition figures have remained largely in the background during the confrontations.
Three leaders of the ex-communist Socialists met Berisha on Tuesday, but both sides reported no progress towards a political solution.
The opposition dismissed the resignation of deeply unpopular Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi as cosmetic and called for a new government of technocrats.
Berisha rejected any coalition with the Socialists and said his earlier attempts at compromise had been interpreted as a sign of weakness and encouraged the rebellion.

Under emergency regulations approved by parliament last weekend, opposition newspapers have yet to secure permission to publish and Tirana residents can read only the Democratic Party daily Rilinda Demokratike.
The offices of the most popular and acerbic opposition daily, Koha Jone, was gutted last Sunday after the state of emergency was introduced.
Opposition leaders rarely get air time on state television, by far the most influential news medium in Europe's poorest country. It devotes many news reports to the activities of the government.

The Socialists last year pointedly distanced themselves from the 45-year rule of terror, suspicion and isolation under dictator Enver Hoxha when they formally ditched Marxist ideology and declared themselves to be in the tradition of western Social Democratic parties.
They have denied instigating violence and insist they will use only political means to resolve the crisis.

But with its chief Fatos Nano in jail since 1994 on corruption charges, the Socialist Party has produced no leaders either with mass appeal or capable of coming up with a plan to haul the country out of economic crisis.
The Socialists have been upstaged since the onset of violence by two smaller parties within the Forum, the centre-left Social Democrats and the Democratic Alliance to their right.
Their leaders have made high-profile appearances at demonstrations in Tirana and Vlore, the southern port where the most violent clashes have occurred.
